lesson.title: Finding Out What Is Really in There: An Overview of Chemical Analysis
lesson.summary: Chemical analysis answers two different questions about a sample, what is present, answered by qualitative analysis, and how much of it is present, answered by quantitative techniques such as volumetric and gravimetric analysis, and combining both is the standard approach to fully characterizing an unknown sample.
lesson.body:
Chemical analysis is the general process of figuring out the composition of a sample, and it splits naturally into two different kinds of questions. Qualitative analysis asks what substances or ions are present at all, without worrying yet about quantity. A familiar qualitative test is adding AgNO3 to an unknown solution: an immediate white precipitate forming is strong evidence that chloride ion is present, since silver chloride is one of the classic insoluble metathesis products covered earlier in this unit. That test tells you chloride is there, but it says nothing yet about how much.

Answering how much requires quantitative analysis. Volumetric analysis is one major quantitative approach, most commonly performed as a titration, in which a solution of precisely known concentration, the standard solution or titrant, is added to the unknown until the reaction between them reaches its stoichiometric endpoint. The volume of titrant used, combined with its known molarity and the mole ratio from the balanced equation, lets you calculate exactly how much of the unknown was present, using the same molar-ratio bridge introduced at the start of this unit. A second major quantitative approach is gravimetric analysis, which converts the substance of interest into an insoluble solid of precisely known composition, often through exactly the kind of precipitation reaction covered in the metathesis chapter, then filters, dries, and weighs that solid to work backward to the original amount.

Here is a worked example that combines both ideas. A 0.500 g sample of impure table salt is dissolved in water, and adding an excess of AgNO3 produces an immediate white precipitate, the qualitative confirmation that chloride ion is present. That precipitate is filtered, dried completely, and weighed, giving a mass of 0.775 g of AgCl. What mass percent of the original sample was chloride?

The molar mass of AgCl is 107.87 g/mol for silver plus 35.45 g/mol for chlorine, which is 143.32 g/mol. The moles of AgCl obtained are 0.775 g divided by 143.32 g/mol, which equals 0.00541 mol. Because the mole ratio between AgCl and Cl- is 1 to 1, the sample also contained 0.00541 mol of chloride. Converting to mass, 0.00541 mol times 35.45 g/mol equals 0.192 g of chloride. Dividing by the original sample mass and multiplying by 100 gives the mass percent: (0.192 g divided by 0.500 g) times 100%, which equals 38.3% chloride by mass.

This two-step pattern, a qualitative test to confirm what is present followed by a quantitative measurement to determine how much, is the backbone of essentially all chemical analysis. It also sets up exactly the situation the next chapter addresses: what happens when the substance you actually want to measure cannot be titrated directly, which is precisely when back titration becomes the tool of choice.
